longForm.title: The Arrow Storm: How the Battle of Crécy Unmade French Chivalry
longForm.excerpt: On 26 August 1346, Edward III's longbowmen shattered fifteen French cavalry charges on a ridge in Normandy. What happened at Crécy that evening changed European warfare for a century.
paragraphs: The evening of 26 August 1346 was broken by the sound of English longbows. Edward III had chosen his ground on a ridge above the village of Crécy-en-Ponthieu, in northern France, three weeks after landing an army in Normandy and marching it through the country as methodically as a burning match. He had positioned his three divisions on the slope. The French were coming from the west. The sun would be in their eyes.

Edward had been raiding since July 12, when his fleet put approximately 15,000 men ashore at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy. The campaign was a chevauchée — a deliberate scorching of the land meant to humiliate Philip VI and demonstrate that the French king could not protect his own subjects. Edward burned Caen. He drove to within twenty miles of Paris before turning north, pursued by a French army that outweighed his considerably. The French had been unable to bring him to battle on ground they controlled. At Crécy, he stopped running.

The English position was well chosen. The ridge gave Edward's archers elevation and a clear field of fire. He divided his force into three battles: the right wing under the sixteen-year-old Edward of Woodstock — the Black Prince — the left under the Earl of Northampton, and a reserve under the king himself, watching from a windmill on the crest. Welsh and English longbowmen anchored both flanks. An English archer could release ten to twelve arrows per minute. A Genoese crossbowman — the best crossbowmen in Europe — could manage two to three bolts. Philip VI had around six thousand Genoese in his army, retained at considerable expense, and he sent them forward first.

The Genoese advanced first, down the slope toward the English line. Several things went wrong simultaneously. They had left their pavises — the large shields that protected crossbowmen while they reloaded — with the baggage wagons. They had marched all day and were exhausted. A sharp thunderstorm shortly before the battle had wet the cords of their crossbows and reduced their range. The English archers had unstrung their bows during the storm and protected them. When the Genoese fired several volleys that fell short, the English opened fire. The Genoese broke. According to Froissart, who compiled his account from eyewitnesses and was not squeamish about particulars, Philip's cavalry then rode them down. 'Kill me those rascals,' the French knights allegedly said, 'for they stop up our road without any reason.' The precise words are almost certainly invented. What happened to the Genoese is not.

Philip launched charge after charge against the English line. The accounts differ on how many — Froissart gives fifteen, which later historians consider plausible given the duration of the fighting, which ran into the night by torchlight. Each charge broke on the arrow storm. French knights fell in the killing ground below the ridge in numbers that were not fully counted until morning. Among them, somewhere in the dark, was John of Bohemia, king of a landlocked realm with no direct interest in the quarrel between England and France. John was blind — had been for years. He ordered his knights to tie their horses' reins to his so they could lead him into the battle. He wanted to strike at least one blow with his sword. He died in the field. His device — three ostrich feathers with the motto 'Ich Dien' — was later adopted by the Black Prince. Whether the heraldic connection is legend or record has been disputed. John's death is not.

The Black Prince's division came under severe pressure at some point in the fighting — severe enough that his commanders sent a messenger to Edward III asking for reinforcements. The king's reply has been passed down in various forms. The substance is consistent across accounts. Edward asked if the prince was dead or wounded. He was told the prince was alive and fighting. Then, the king reportedly said, he would not be disturbed on the prince's behalf, because the prince needed to win his spurs himself. The reinforcements were not sent. The Black Prince's line held. Edward III's confidence was either cold-blooded parental calculation or theatre. Possibly both.

By morning the field was surveyed. French dead included, by Froissart's count, at least 1,500 knights and esquires. Modern historians, drawing on French armorial rolls rather than eyewitness tallies, put the noble dead at approximately eleven princes, eighty lords, and around 1,200 knights — figures subject to revision. English casualties are recorded as several hundred. The arithmetic is contested; the asymmetry is not. Philip VI escaped with a small party, reportedly reaching the castle of Labroye at night. 'Open, open, it is the fortune of France,' he is said to have announced at the gate. The gatekeepers opened. The line survives in Froissart. Whether Philip said it is another matter.

The tactical lesson was absorbed and disputed for generations. The longbow's effectiveness at Crécy depended on specific conditions: chosen ground, exhausted Genoese, cavalry charging uphill into the setting sun. English commanders spent the next century trying to replicate those conditions, with varying success. At Agincourt in 1415 they did it again. French military planners spent roughly the same period debating how to break the longbow's dominance and failing to find an answer fast enough. Gunpowder artillery eventually rendered the question moot — but that came later and slowly. At Crécy, Philip had launched fifteen charges. The archers had been there for all of them.

What Crécy changed — and what contemporaries understood it to change — was the relationship between mounted knights and infantry. The mounted charge was the central tactical instrument of medieval European warfare, the expression of a social order in which the man who could afford armor and a warhorse stood above the man who could not. The longbow did not end chivalric warfare in a single afternoon. But it demonstrated, in terms specific enough to count afterward, that common infantry could kill the flower of French aristocracy in quantity and at range. The bill presented at Crécy was paid in noble blood. The social accounting came later and slower. But it had begun.

shortForm.title: Flodden, 1513: The Last King and the Wrong Ground
shortForm.excerpt: James IV of Scotland invaded England with the largest army his kingdom had ever fielded while Henry VIII was in France. Thomas Howard, Earl of Surrey, met him at Flodden Hill. The terrain did the rest.
paragraphs: September 9, 1513. James IV of Scotland had crossed the Tweed at the head of an army estimated between thirty and forty thousand men — the largest force Scotland had put into England in living memory — while Henry VIII was in France besieging Thérouanne. The timing was deliberate. James held a treaty obligation with France and had received French money and equipment. What he had not adequately considered was Thomas Howard, the seventy-year-old Earl of Surrey, who mustered an English force of comparable size and moved north to meet him.

James took a strong position on Flodden Hill, overlooking the River Till. The high ground was sound. Surrey could not attack uphill against the Scottish artillery. He marched his army north and then east, cutting across James's line of retreat toward Scotland. It was a straightforward operational move that forced James off his prepared ground. The Scottish army shifted to Branxton Hill. The maneuver was competently executed. What followed was not.

The Scottish infantry carried eighteen-foot Swiss pikes. On flat ground, in disciplined formation, pike squares were among the most effective infantry systems in Europe. Branxton Hill was not flat. The downhill advance broke the formations. The pikes — designed to be used en masse, with steady footing and dressed ranks — became unwieldy on the slope, and the English bills, shorter weapons with a hook and an axe-blade suited to close-quarter work in broken terrain, went to work on what remained. James IV, who had ridden into the press personally, was killed within yards of the English line. He was the last British monarch to die in battle. Scottish dead included two bishops, twelve earls, and around fifteen lords of parliament; total dead is estimated between eight and ten thousand.

Flodden is not well remembered outside Scotland, where it is called a catastrophe and where the old song 'The Flowers of the Forest' was composed in mourning for the fallen. Military historians have noted that James had a capable army and a sound defensive plan, and allowed both to be undone by terrain he could not control on the advance. His decision to leave Flodden Hill remains debated. The collapse of his pike formation on the slope does not.

onThisDay.headline: Battle of the Coral Sea: US Carrier Aircraft Strike Tulagi
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1942, United States carrier aircraft from USS Yorktown launched the opening strikes of the Battle of the Coral Sea, attacking Japanese forces at Tulagi in the Solomon Islands. The four-day engagement — the first naval battle in history in which opposing surface fleets never came within sight of each other — resulted in the Japanese abandonment of their planned amphibious assault on Port Moresby, New Guinea, the first strategic check to Japanese expansion in the Pacific.
